title: A Table and a Cubic
topic: Function Concepts · Composition, inverses, zeros, and end behavior
prompt: The function \(f\) is increasing and is defined for \(x \ge 0\). The table gives values of \(f(x)\) at selected values of \(x\). The function \(g\) is given by \(g(x) = 0.5x^3 - 2x^2 + 1.2\).

parts.label: A
parts.text: (i) The function \(h\) is defined by \(h(x) = (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))\). Find the value of \(h(1)\), or indicate that it is not defined. Show the work that leads to your answer. (ii) Find the value of \(f^{-1}(10)\), or indicate that it is not defined.

rubricPoints.criterion: Finds \(h(1) = g(f(1)) = g(5) = 13.7\), with supporting work showing \(f(1) = 5\) or \(g(5)\).
commonErrors: gives the value without supporting work

parts.label: B
parts.text: (i) Find all values of \(x\), as decimal approximations, for which \(g(x) = 0\), or indicate that there are no such values. (ii) Determine the end behavior of \(g\) as \(x\) decreases without bound. Express your answer using the mathematical notation of a limit.

commonErrors: reports only one or two zeros
rounds to fewer than three decimal places

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x) = -\infty\).
commonErrors: describes the behavior in words only
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: As \(x\) gets very negative, \(g\) goes down.

parts.label: C
parts.text: (i) Based on the table, which of the following function types best models \(f\): linear, quadratic, exponential, or logarithmic? (ii) Give a reason for your answer based on the relationship between the change in the output values of \(f\) and the change in the input values of \(f\). Refer to values in the table.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies quadratic.
commonErrors: identifies exponential because the values grow quickly

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that over equal-length input intervals the first differences (3, 5, 7, 9) change by a constant amount (second differences all 2), so the rate of change changes at a constant rate.
commonErrors: refers only to a regression or r²
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Over input intervals of length 1, the output changes are 3, 5, 7, 9, which increase by 2 each time; constant second differences mean quadratic.

sampleResponse: A (i) \(h(1) = g(f(1)) = g(5) = 0.5(125) - 2(25) + 1.2 = 13.7\). (ii) \(f(2) = 10\), so \(f^{-1}(10) = 2\). B (i) \(x = -0.713,\ 0.876,\ 3.836\). (ii) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x) = -\infty\). C (i) Quadratic. (ii) On input intervals of length 1, the changes in output are 3, 5, 7, 9; these increase by a constant 2, so the second differences are constant and a quadratic model is best.

title: Reservoir Level During a Drought
topic: Modeling a Non-Periodic Context · Quadratic model, secant line, and domain

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Precalculus Question 2 (Modeling a Non-Periodic Context)

prompt: During a drought, engineers record the depth of water in a reservoir. At \(t = 0\) months the depth was 120 feet, at \(t = 3\) months it was 105 feet, and at \(t = 6\) months it was 96 feet. The depth can be modeled by \(W(t) = at^2 + bt + c\), where \(W(t)\) is the depth in feet and \(t\) is measured in months.

figures.caption: Table
figures.alt: Table: t (months) 0, Depth (feet) 120; t (months) 3, Depth (feet) 105; t (months) 6, Depth (feet) 96

parts.label: A
parts.text: (i) Use the given data to write three equations that can be used to find the values of \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\). (ii) Find the values of \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) as decimal approximations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes three equations using the data: \(c = 120\), \(9a + 3b + c = 105\), \(36a + 6b + c = 96\).

parts.label: B
parts.text: (i) Use the given data to find the average rate of change of the depth, in feet per month, from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 6\). Show the computations. (ii) Use this average rate of change to estimate the depth at \(t = 2\). Show the work. (iii) Let \(A_t\) be the estimate of the depth found using the average rate of change from part B (i). Explain why \(A_t > W(t)\) for all \(t\) with \(0 < t < 6\). Refer to the graph of \(W\) and its relationship to \(A_t\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Computes \(\dfrac{96 - 120}{6 - 0} = -4\) feet per month, with a difference quotient shown.
Estimates \(120 + (-4)(2) = 112\) feet (or a value consistent with part B (i)).
commonErrors: uses the model instead of the secant line

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that A_t lies on the secant line through (0, W(0)) and (6, W(6)), and since the graph of W is concave up on 0 < t < 6, the secant line lies above the graph.
commonErrors: does not mention the secant line
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A_t is on the secant line from t = 0 to t = 6. W is concave up there (a > 0), so the secant line lies above the graph of W.

parts.label: C
parts.text: The quadratic model W has exactly one absolute minimum or absolute maximum. Engineers know that the depth cannot increase until the rainy season begins, after the time period being modeled. Explain how the minimum or maximum can be used to determine a boundary for the domain of W.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that \(W\) has an absolute minimum (at \(t = 9\)) and increases afterward, but the depth cannot increase, so the domain must end at the time of the minimum.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: W decreases until its minimum at t = 9 and then increases. Since the depth cannot rise during the drought, the model applies only up to t = 9.

sampleResponse: A (i) \(c = 120\); \(9a + 3b + c = 105\); \(36a + 6b + c = 96\). (ii) \(9a + 3b = -15\) and \(36a + 6b = -24\) give \(a = 0.333\), \(b = -6\), \(c = 120\). B (i) \(\dfrac{96 - 120}{6} = -4\) feet per month. (ii) \(120 - 4(2) = 112\) feet. (iii) \(A_t\) is on the secant line through \((0, W(0))\) and \((6, W(6))\). Because \(W\) is concave up on \(0 < t < 6\), the secant line lies above the graph of \(W\), so \(A_t > W(t)\). C \(W\) has an absolute minimum at \(t = 9\) and increases after it. The depth cannot increase during the drought, so the domain of \(W\) should have right endpoint \(t = 9\).

figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: The graph of \(h\) and its dashed midline for two full cycles is shown in Figure 1. Five points, F, G, J, K, and P, are labeled. No scale is indicated, and no axes are presented. Determine possible coordinates \((t, h(t))\) for the five points.

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives correct \(h(t)\)-coordinates: \(-0.8, 0, 0.8, 0, -0.8\).
Gives correct \(t\)-coordinates: \(0, 1, 2, 3, 4\) (or shifted by a multiple of 4).

parts.label: B
parts.text: The function \(h\) can be written in the form \(h(t) = a\sin(b(t + c)) + d\). Find values of the constants \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), and \(d\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives correct vertical transformations: \(a = 0.8\) with \(d = 0\) (or \(a = -0.8\), \(d = 0\)).
Gives correct horizontal transformations: \(b = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(c = -1\) (or \(c = 3\); with \(a = -0.8\), \(c = 1\)).

parts.label: C
parts.text: Refer to the graph in part A. The \(t\)-coordinate of G is \(t_1\), and the \(t\)-coordinate of J is \(t_2\). (i) On the interval \((t_1, t_2)\), which is true about \(h\)? (a) positive and increasing (b) positive and decreasing (c) negative and increasing (d) negative and decreasing. (ii) On \((t_1, t_2)\), describe the concavity of the graph of \(h\) and determine whether the rate of change of \(h\) is increasing or decreasing.

rubricPoints.criterion: Chooses (a): positive and increasing.
commonErrors: chooses negative because the buoy started below

rubricPoints.criterion: States that the graph is concave down and the rate of change of h is decreasing.
commonErrors: says increasing at an increasing rate
gives only one of the two descriptions
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Concave down; the rate of change of h is decreasing.

sampleResponse: A F(0, −0.8), G(1, 0), J(2, 0.8), K(3, 0), P(4, −0.8). B \(a = 0.8\), \(b = \dfrac{2\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(c = -1\), \(d = 0\), so \(h(t) = 0.8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}(t - 1)\right)\). C (i) (a) positive and increasing. (ii) The graph is concave down, and the rate of change of \(h\) is decreasing.

title: Logs, Sines, and Powers of 2
topic: Symbolic Manipulations · Equations and equivalent forms
prompt: Directions: Unless otherwise specified, the domain of a function is all real numbers for which it is defined, and angles are in radians. Give exact values for expressions that can be found without a calculator, combine terms using algebra and the rules for exponents and logarithms where applicable, and show the work that leads to each answer.

parts.label: A
parts.text: The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are given by \(g(x) = 3\log_2 x\) and \(h(x) = 4\sin^2 x\). (i) Solve \(g(x) = 9\) for values of \(x\) in the domain of \(g\). (ii) Solve \(h(x) = 3\) for values of \(x\) in the interval \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Solves to \(x = 8\) with supporting work (\(\log_2 x = 3\), so \(x = 2^3\)).
Solves to \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) with supporting work (\(\sin x = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)).

parts.label: B
parts.text: The functions \(j\) and \(k\) are given by \(j(x) = \ln x - 2\ln 3\) and \(k(x) = \dfrac{3(1 - \sin^2 x)}{\cos x}\). (i) Rewrite \(j(x)\) as a single natural logarithm without negative exponents, in the form \(\ln(\text{expression})\). (ii) Rewrite \(k(x)\) as an expression in which \(\cos x\) appears exactly once and no other trigonometric functions are involved.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(j(x) = \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{9}\right)\).
Writes \(k(x) = 3\cos x\) using the Pythagorean identity, with supporting work.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: \(1 - \sin^2 x = \cos^2 x\), so \(k(x) = \dfrac{3\cos^2 x}{\cos x} = 3\cos x\).

parts.label: C
parts.text: The function \(m\) is given by \(m(x) = 4^x - 6\cdot 2^x + 8\). Find all input values in the domain of \(m\) that yield an output value of 0.

rubricPoints.criterion: Rewrites in quadratic form with \(y = 2^x\) and factors: \((y - 2)(y - 4) = 0\).
Finds \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\), with no incorrect values.

sampleResponse: A (i) \(3\log_2 x = 9 \Rightarrow \log_2 x = 3 \Rightarrow x = 8\). (ii) \(4\sin^2 x = 3 \Rightarrow \sin x = \pm\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\); in \([0, \tfrac{\pi}{2})\), \(x = \tfrac{\pi}{3}\). B (i) \(j(x) = \ln x - \ln 9 = \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{9}\right)\). (ii) \(k(x) = \dfrac{3\cos^2 x}{\cos x} = 3\cos x\). C Let \(y = 2^x\): \(y^2 - 6y + 8 = (y - 2)(y - 4) = 0\), so \(2^x = 2\) or \(2^x = 4\), giving \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\).

parts.label: A
parts.text: (i) The function \(h\) is defined by \(h(x) = g(f(x))\). Find the value of \(h(2)\) as a decimal approximation, or indicate that it is not defined. Show the work. (ii) Find all values of \(x\) for which \(f(x) = 5\), or indicate that there are no such values.

rubricPoints.criterion: Finds \(h(2) = g(f(2)) = g(2) \approx -0.525\) (or \(-0.526\)), with supporting work.
Finds \(x = -2\).

parts.label: B
parts.text: (i) Find all values of \(x\), as decimal approximations, for which \(g(x) = -3\), or indicate that there are no such values. (ii) Determine the behavior of \(g\) as \(x\) decreases without bound. Express your answer using the mathematical notation of a limit.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x) = 1.7\).

parts.label: C
parts.text: (i) Is the function \(f\) invertible? (ii) Give a reason for your answer based on properties of \(f\). Refer to points on the graph of \(f\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Answers yes.
commonErrors: answers no because the graph is made of segments

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that f is decreasing on its whole domain, so no two inputs share an output, citing points on the graph (for example, outputs fall from 8 at x = −4 to −1 at x = 4 without repeating).
commonErrors: says only “passes the horizontal line test”
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: f decreases from (−4, 8) through (0, 3) to (4, −1), so every output occurs for exactly one input.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: It passes the horizontal line test.

sampleResponse: A (i) \(h(2) = g(f(2)) = g(2) = 1.7 - e^{0.8} \approx -0.525\). (ii) \(f(-2) = 5\), so \(x = -2\). B (i) \(1.7 - e^{0.4x} = -3 \Rightarrow e^{0.4x} = 4.7 \Rightarrow x \approx 3.869\). (ii) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x) = 1.7\). C (i) Yes. (ii) \(f\) is decreasing on its domain, falling from \((-4, 8)\) through \((0, 3)\) to \((4, -1)\), so no output value is repeated; each output comes from exactly one input.

title: An Invasive Fish Population
topic: Modeling a Non-Periodic Context · Exponential model, secant line, and domain

modeledOn.label: 2026 AP Precalculus Question 2 (Modeling a Non-Periodic Context)

prompt: An invasive fish species was discovered in a lake. Two years after the discovery (\(t = 2\)), biologists estimated 1.8 thousand fish; five years after the discovery (\(t = 5\)), they estimated 4.2 thousand fish. The population can be modeled by \(F(t) = ab^t\), where \(F(t)\) is the number of fish, in thousands, and \(t\) is the number of years since the discovery.

parts.label: A
parts.text: (i) Use the given data to write two equations that can be used to find the values of \(a\) and \(b\). (ii) Find the values of \(a\) and \(b\) as decimal approximations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Finds \(b \approx 1.326\) and \(a \approx 1.023\).
commonErrors: takes the square root instead of the cube root

parts.label: B
parts.text: (i) Use the given data to find the average rate of change of the population, in thousands of fish per year, from \(t = 2\) to \(t = 5\). Show the computations. (ii) Use this average rate of change to estimate the population at \(t = 3\). (iii) Let \(A(t)\) be the estimate from the secant line through \((2, F(2))\) and \((5, F(5))\). It can be shown that \(A(3) > F(3)\). Use the secant line and the graph of \(F\) to explain why \(A(t) > F(t)\) for all \(t\) with \(2 < t < 5\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Computes \(\dfrac{4.2 - 1.8}{5 - 2} = 0.8\) thousand fish per year with a difference quotient.
Estimates \(1.8 + 0.8(1) = 2.6\) thousand fish (or a value consistent with part B (i)).
Explains that F is concave up (b > 1, its rate of change is increasing), so the secant line on 2 < t < 5 lies above the graph of F.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: An increasing exponential with b > 1 is concave up, so on 2 < t < 5 the secant line lies above the graph and A(t) > F(t).

parts.label: C
parts.text: Biologists estimate that the lake can support at most 20 thousand fish of this species. Explain how this information can be used to determine a domain limitation for the model F.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that \(F\) increases without bound, but the population cannot exceed 20 thousand, so the model applies only for \(t \le k\), where \(F(k) = 20\) (\(k \approx 10.5\) years).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: F keeps increasing, so the model can only apply until F(k) = 20, about k = 10.5 years; the domain is [0, k].

sampleResponse: A (i) \(ab^2 = 1.8\) and \(ab^5 = 4.2\). (ii) \(b^3 = \tfrac{4.2}{1.8}\), so \(b \approx 1.326\) and \(a = 1.8/b^2 \approx 1.023\). B (i) \(\dfrac{4.2 - 1.8}{5 - 2} = 0.8\) thousand fish per year. (ii) \(1.8 + 0.8(3 - 2) = 2.6\) thousand fish. (iii) \(F\) is an increasing exponential with \(b > 1\), so its graph is concave up; the secant line through \((2, F(2))\) and \((5, F(5))\) lies above the graph on \(2 < t < 5\), so \(A(t) > F(t)\). C \(F\) increases without bound, but the lake can hold at most 20 thousand fish, so the model only applies up to the time \(k\) with \(F(k) = 20\), about \(k = 10.53\) years.

figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: The graph of \(h\) and its dashed midline for two full cycles is shown in Figure 1. Five points, F, G, J, K, and P, are labeled. No scale is indicated, and no axes are presented. Determine possible coordinates \((t, h(t))\) for the five points.

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives correct \(h(t)\)-coordinates: 55, 30, 5, 30, 55.
commonErrors: uses heights relative to the center (25, 0, −25)

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives correct \(t\)-coordinates: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (or shifted by a multiple of 8).

parts.label: B
parts.text: The function \(h\) can be written in the form \(h(t) = a\sin(b(t + c)) + d\). Find values of the constants \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), and \(d\).

parts.label: C
parts.text: Refer to the graph in part A. The \(t\)-coordinate of J is \(t_1\), and the \(t\)-coordinate of K is \(t_2\). (i) On the interval \((t_1, t_2)\), which is true about \(h\)? (a) positive and increasing (b) positive and decreasing (c) negative and increasing (d) negative and decreasing. (ii) On \((t_1, t_2)\), describe the concavity of the graph of \(h\) and determine whether the rate of change of \(h\) is increasing or decreasing.

rubricPoints.criterion: Chooses (a): positive and increasing (heights above the ground are positive).
commonErrors: chooses (c) by measuring from the center

rubricPoints.criterion: States that the graph is concave up and the rate of change of h is increasing.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Concave up; the rate of change of h is increasing.

sampleResponse: A F(0, 55), G(2, 30), J(4, 5), K(6, 30), P(8, 55). B \(a = 25\), \(b = \dfrac{2\pi}{8} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(c = 2\), \(d = 30\), so \(h(t) = 25\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}(t + 2)\right) + 30\). C (i) (a) positive and increasing. (ii) The graph is concave up, and the rate of change of \(h\) is increasing.

title: Exponents, Logs, and a Double Angle
prompt: Directions: Unless otherwise specified, the domain of a function is all real numbers for which it is defined, and angles are in radians. Give exact values for expressions that can be found without a calculator, combine terms using algebra and the rules for exponents and logarithms where applicable, and show the work that leads to each answer.

parts.label: A
parts.text: The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are given by \(g(x) = 9^x\) and \(h(x) = \log_5(2x + 1)\). (i) Solve \(g(x) = \dfrac{1}{27}\) for values of \(x\) in the domain of \(g\). (ii) Solve \(h(x) = 2\) for values of \(x\) in the domain of \(h\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Solves to \(x = -\tfrac{3}{2}\) with supporting work (rewriting both sides as powers of 3).
Solves to \(x = 12\) with supporting work.

parts.label: B
parts.text: The functions \(j\) and \(k\) are given by \(j(x) = (2^{x-1})^3 \cdot 2^x\) and \(k(x) = \dfrac{1 - \cos(2x)}{2\sin x}\). (i) Rewrite \(j(x)\) in the form \(2^{(\text{expression})}\). (ii) Rewrite \(k(x)\) as an expression in which \(\sin x\) appears exactly once and no other trigonometric functions are involved.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(k(x) = \sin x\) using \(1 - \cos(2x) = 2\sin^2 x\), with supporting work.

parts.label: C
parts.text: The function \(m\) is given by \(m(x) = 4\sin^2(2x) - 3\). Find all input values in the interval \([0, \pi]\) that yield an output value of 0.

rubricPoints.criterion: Finds a correct value of \(2x\) (or \(x\)) for which \(\sin(2x) = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), such as \(2x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).
commonErrors: solves sin x instead of sin 2x

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives all four values \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) with no incorrect values.
commonErrors: misses the solutions from the negative root

sampleResponse: A (i) \(3^{2x} = 3^{-3} \Rightarrow x = -\tfrac{3}{2}\). (ii) \(2x + 1 = 25 \Rightarrow x = 12\). B (i) \(j(x) = 2^{3x - 3}\cdot 2^x = 2^{4x - 3}\). (ii) \(k(x) = \dfrac{2\sin^2 x}{2\sin x} = \sin x\). C \(\sin^2(2x) = \tfrac{3}{4}\), so \(\sin(2x) = \pm\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). For \(0 \le 2x \le 2\pi\): \(2x = \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{2\pi}{3}, \tfrac{4\pi}{3}, \tfrac{5\pi}{3}\), so \(x = \tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{2\pi}{3}, \tfrac{5\pi}{6}\).
